“The I is satanic by nature and unsociable by character. In Hell there is no pronoun except ‘I.’” That would make a beautiful illustration for Stirner’s The Ego and Its Own. I already knew this unconsciously in 1908. But between 1905 and 1907 it was confused by the philosophy of the “I” inherited from the German educational tradition and by Kluxen’s boasting. That is also why Stirner impressed me back then: as the swaggerer of the I, the boor of the I, the consistently nihilistic I.

My sympathy for two outstanding canon lawyers, Teodoro Andrés Marcos and Hans Barion, reveals the whole unhappy incompleteness of my position between theologians and lawyers of secular law. There are no better lawyers than us. But we are crushed between theology and technology. Those two canon lawyers are jurists of theology. I am a theologian of jurisprudence.
The result is failure in an age of massive secularity, cast-iron concepts, and the most delicate and cautious forms of indirect power.
